## Agent-based models — Day 3, Session 1

Worksheet: `worksheets/09-agent-based-models.qmd`. The chapter is
[Agent-based models](../chapters/09-agent-based-models.qmd).

Every run is seeded with `StableRNG`, which fixes the random stream but not what
`shuffle`, `Poisson` sampling and `rand(rng, collection)` draw from it, so the
digits below hold for the course's pinned package set. Here `check` raises an
error rather than printing a cross, so a failed validation stops the render
instead of sitting above a set of published numbers.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-setup
using Agents
using CairoMakie
using Distributions
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using Random
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

function check(name, condition)
    condition || error("check failed: $name")
    println("✓ $name")
    return nothing
end

no_steps!(model) = nothing   # for demonstration grids that are never stepped

N = 1000
β = 0.05
c = 10.0
γ = 0.25
horizon = 120.0

println("R₀ under mass action = ", β * c / γ)
```

### Part A — the three components

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a2
@agent struct Person(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end
```

`@agent` copies in the fields a two-dimensional grid agent needs, `id` and `pos`,
and adds the two asked for. It is not inheritance: `Person` gets no methods from
`GridAgent{2}`, and the rules arrive separately in Part C as ordinary functions.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a1
space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a3
function initialize_model(seed; I0 = 10, radius = 2, Δt = 0.1)
    space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person, space;
        agent_step!, model_step!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt, radius = radius),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for position in positions(model)
        add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:I0]
        model[id].status = :I
        model[id].next_status = :I
    end
    return model
end
```

### Part B — the neighbourhood

A diagonal neighbour is one Chebyshev step away, the same as a neighbour directly
above, so radius 1 under that metric is the full ring of eight.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b1
neighbourhood_radius = 1
neighbourhood_metric = :chebyshev

function demo_grid(metric)
    demo = StandardABM(
        Person, GridSpaceSingle((9, 9); periodic = false, metric = metric);
        model_step! = no_steps!,   # this grid is only for looking at
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = 0.1, radius = 1),
        rng = StableRNG(1),
    )
    for position in positions(demo)
        add_agent!(position, demo; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    return demo
end

demo = demo_grid(neighbourhood_metric)
centre = (5, 5)
neighbourhood = collect(nearby_positions(centre, demo, neighbourhood_radius))

check("the neighbourhood holds eight cells", length(neighbourhood) == 8)
check("every one of them touches the centre cell",
      !isempty(neighbourhood) &&
      all(maximum(abs.(p .- centre)) == 1 for p in neighbourhood))

(; neighbourhood_radius, neighbourhood_metric, size = length(neighbourhood))
```

Under `:euclidean` a radius of 1 gives only the four cells sharing an edge, and a
radius of 2 reaches past the ring to the cells two steps away. Neither is the
Moore neighbourhood, which is why the metric has to be named rather than assumed.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-neighbourhood
#| fig-cap: "One person (black) on a nine-by-nine grid with the cells within Chebyshev radius 1 (dark red) and the further cells added at radius 2 (orange). Radius 1 is the eight people touching the focal person; radius 2 adds sixteen more, twenty-four in all."

focal = picture[id_in_position(centre, picture)]
ring1 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, picture, 1))
ring2 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, picture, 2))

                     agent_size = 26, figure = (; size = (520, 520)))
hidedecorations!(ax)
ax.title = "Radius 1 and radius 2 under the Chebyshev metric"

```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b2
function corner_neighbours(periodic)
    grid = StandardABM(
        Person, GridSpaceSingle((9, 9); periodic = periodic, metric = :chebyshev);
        model_step! = no_steps!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = 0.1, radius = 1),
        rng = StableRNG(1),
    )
    for position in positions(grid)
        add_agent!(position, grid; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    return length(collect(nearby_positions((1, 1), grid, 1)))
end

(; wrapped = corner_neighbours(true), with_edges = corner_neighbours(false))
```

#### B1. Interpret

- With edges rather than wrapping, a corner person has three neighbours where a
  person in the middle has eight. That does not make the corner safer under this
  rule. The number of contact attempts is $\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$
  wherever you live and each lands on a neighbour drawn uniformly, so the risk
  per contact is the *proportion* infectious in the neighbourhood: one infectious
  neighbour out of three carries $8/3$ times the hazard of one out of eight.
- That is frequency-dependent transmission carried over from the well-mixed
  model, a consequence of holding $c$ fixed as the pool shrinks rather than a fact
  about grids. Fixing the per-neighbour hazard instead, so that each infectious
  neighbour transmits with probability $1-\exp(-\beta c\Delta t/n_0)$ for a
  reference size $n_0$, gives the same answer on a full neighbourhood and scales
  risk down at an edge rather than up.
- A boundary also caps how many distinct people a corner infective can reach and
  stops a front of infection at the edge. Those effects pull in different
  directions, so whether a bounded grid gives a larger or smaller epidemic has to
  be measured.
- Wrapping gives every person exactly eight neighbours at radius 1 and
  twenty-four at radius 2, so variation between people comes from the epidemic
  and not from where they live. A wrapped grid is unrealistic, but its unrealism
  is the same everywhere.

### Part C — the rules

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c1
function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        neighbours = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius))
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbours)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I
        if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
            person.next_status = :R
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

function model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
    return nothing
end

susceptible_count(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
recovered_count(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c2
function simulate(seed; I0 = 10, radius = 2, Δt = 0.1)
    steps = round(Int, horizon / Δt)
    _, data = run!(
        initialize_model(seed; I0, radius, Δt), steps;
        mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return Matrix(data[:, [
        :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count,
    ]])'
end

single_run = simulate(20250711)
step_times = collect(0.0:0.1:horizon)

check("every person has exactly one status at every step",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(single_run; dims = 1)) .- N)) == 0)
check("counts are whole people and never negative", minimum(single_run) >= 0)
check("the epidemic took off", single_run[3, end] > 100)
check("the epidemic has finished by the end of the run", single_run[2, end] == 0)

(; final_counts = single_run[:, end],
   peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]),
   peak_time = step_times[argmax(single_run[2, :])])
```

```{julia}
                   p.status === :I ? :firebrick : :seagreen

snapshot_model = initialize_model(20250711)
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 250))

for (j, t) in enumerate((5.0, 20.0, 50.0))
    step!(snapshot_model, round(Int, (t - previous) / 0.1))
    previous = t
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t", aspect = DataAspect())
    abmplot!(ax, snapshot_model; agent_color = status_colour,
             agent_marker = :rect, agent_size = 7)
    hidedecorations!(ax)
end
fig
```

The transmission rule is the ODE's rule applied one person at a time. A
susceptible drawing $K\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ contacts, each
infecting with probability $\beta$, escapes infection over one step with
probability

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(1-\beta p)^{K}\right] = e^{-\beta c \Delta t\, p},
$$

where $p$ is the proportion infectious among the people it can reach. That is the
ODE's force of infection $\beta c I/N$ exactly, provided $p = I/N$. Drawing from
the whole population makes it so; drawing from 24 fixed neighbours does not.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c3
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    b, contact, g, n = p
    infection = b * contact * u[1] * u[2] / n
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - g * u[2]
    du[3] = g * u[2]
    return nothing
end

ode_solution = solve(
    ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, horizon), (β, c, γ, N)),
    Tsit5(); saveat = step_times,
)
ode_states = Array(ode_solution)

(; abm_peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]),
   ode_peak = round(maximum(ode_states[2, :]); digits = 1),
   abm_final = single_run[3, end],
   ode_final = round(ode_states[3, end]; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}

#| fig-cap: "Three seeded runs of the grid model (solid) against the deterministic SIR trajectory (dashed). The three runs differ from each other, and all three fall well short of the ODE."
seeds = 20250711 .+ (0:2)
replicates = [simulate(seed) for seed in seeds]

fig = Figure(size = (900, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious people",
          title = "Three runs on the grid, and the well-mixed ODE")
for (k, run) in enumerate(replicates)
    lines!(ax, step_times, run[2, :]; color = (:firebrick, 0.8), linewidth = 2,
           label = k == 1 ? "grid model" : nothing)
end

       linewidth = 2, label = "ODE")

fig
```

The control keeps every line of the rules, the grid, the people and the
parameters, and changes only the contact draw, to `random_agent(model)`.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c3a
function well_mixed_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = random_agent(model)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I
        if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
            person.next_status = :R
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

function initialize_well_mixed(seed; I0 = 10, Δt = 0.1)
    space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person, space;
        agent_step! = well_mixed_step!, model_step!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt, radius = 2),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for position in positions(model)
        add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:I0]
        model[id].status = :I
        model[id].next_status = :I
    end
    return model
end

function simulate_well_mixed(seed; I0 = 10, Δt = 0.1)
    steps = round(Int, horizon / Δt)
    _, data = run!(
        initialize_well_mixed(seed; I0, Δt), steps;
        mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return Matrix(data[:, [
        :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count,
    ]])'
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c3b
control_seeds = 20250711 .+ (0:7)
well_mixed_runs = [simulate_well_mixed(seed) for seed in control_seeds]
grid_runs = [simulate(seed) for seed in control_seeds]

mean_curve(runs) = mean(r[2, :] for r in runs)
mean_final(runs) = mean(r[3, end] for r in runs)

ode_peak = maximum(ode_states[2, :])
ode_final = ode_states[3, end]

check("the well-mixed ABM reproduces the ODE peak within 5%",
      abs(maximum(mean_curve(well_mixed_runs)) - ode_peak) / ode_peak < 0.05)
check("the well-mixed ABM reproduces the ODE final size within 5%",
      abs(mean_final(well_mixed_runs) - ode_final) / ode_final < 0.05)
check("the grid model misses the ODE peak by more than 20%",
      abs(maximum(mean_curve(grid_runs)) - ode_peak) / ode_peak > 0.2)
check("every run reached zero infectious before the horizon",
      all(r[2, end] == 0 for r in vcat(well_mixed_runs, grid_runs)))

control_comparison = [(; contacts = name,
    peak_of_mean_curve = round(maximum(mean_curve(runs)); digits = 1),
    mean_final_size = round(mean_final(runs); digits = 1),
    rmse_vs_ode = round(sqrt(mean((mean_curve(runs) .- ode_states[2, :]).^2)); digits = 1))
    for (name, runs) in (("whole population", well_mixed_runs),
                         ("24 neighbours", grid_runs))]
```

The timestep sweep runs six seeds at each setting, downwards as well as upwards,
and `finished` records whether each run had run out of infectious people by the
horizon.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c4
timestep_seeds = 20250711 .+ (0:5)

function timestep_summary(Δt)
    runs = [simulate(seed; Δt = Δt) for seed in timestep_seeds]
    peaks = [maximum(r[2, :]) for r in runs]
    finals = [r[3, end] for r in runs]
    return (; Δt,
              finished = all(r[2, end] == 0 for r in runs),
              mean_peak = round(mean(peaks); digits = 1),
              mean_final = round(mean(finals); digits = 1),
              final_range = extrema(finals),
              final_sd = round(std(finals); digits = 1),
              finals = Float64.(finals))
end

timestep_comparison = [timestep_summary(Δt) for Δt in (0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 1.0)]

check("every timestep run reached zero infectious before the horizon",
      all(row.finished for row in timestep_comparison))

[(; row.Δt, row.finished, row.mean_peak, row.mean_final, row.final_range, row.final_sd)
 for row in timestep_comparison]
```

A shared seed places the same ten starting infectives before any stepping, so
the settings are paired on initial conditions and the uncertainty of a contrast
comes from the seed-wise differences.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c4b
finals_at = Dict(row.Δt => row.finals for row in timestep_comparison)

function paired_contrast(coarse, fine)
    differences = finals_at[coarse] .- finals_at[fine]
    n = length(differences)
    return (; contrast = "Δt = $coarse minus Δt = $fine",
              mean_difference = round(mean(differences); digits = 1),
              paired_se = round(std(differences) / sqrt(n); digits = 1),
              independent_se = round(sqrt(var(finals_at[coarse]) / n +
                                          var(finals_at[fine]) / n); digits = 1),
              correlation = round(cor(finals_at[coarse], finals_at[fine]); digits = 3))
end

timestep_contrasts = [paired_contrast(1.0, 0.1), paired_contrast(0.025, 0.1)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c5
[(; seed, peak = maximum(r[2, :]), peak_time = step_times[argmax(r[2, :])],
    final = r[3, end])
 for (seed, r) in zip(seeds, replicates)]
```

#### C1. Interpret

- The two-phase update keeps activation order out of the model. Writing
  `person.status` directly would let someone infected early in a sweep infect a
  later person in the same $\Delta t$, depending on an ordering with no meaning in
  the model, and the default `Schedulers.fastest` order is not even documented.
  Committing in `model_step!` makes every agent in a step read the same state.
- The three runs peak at 76, 87 and 86 and end with 616, 766 and 652 recovered;
  the ODE peaks at 158.5 and ends at 800.2. The spread between runs is Monte Carlo
  variation, much of it in timing (peaks at $t = 17.6$, $41.6$ and $21.5$). The gap
  to the ODE is not: contacts are spent on neighbours who have already had the
  infection, and no number of replicates removes that.
- With contacts from the whole population the ABM mean peaks at 156.8 against
  158.5 and ends at 812.1 against 800.2, an RMSE of 8.4 people; from twenty-four
  neighbours the same numbers are 77.4, 688.4 and 28.9. Only the contact draw
  differs, so the rest of the code is exonerated and the gap is located in that
  one line.
- A passing control does not show the contact draw is *right*. A wrong radius, a
  diamond metric, a grid that fails to wrap or a neighbour set holding the focal
  person would all pass it. `ws-ch06-c3c` covers that gap by testing the
  neighbourhood directly: uniform degree 24 and 8 pins radius, metric and
  wrapping, and self-exclusion and symmetry rule out two more faults.
- This is the general move for a model with no analytic reference: find a limit
  that has one, check it, then restore the one ingredient under study and
  attribute what changes to it. Agreement to a per cent or two is what a pass
  looks like at 1000 people, and the peak of the mean curve sits below the typical
  single-run peak, because averaging at fixed clock time flattens peaks that fall
  at different times.
- The mean peak falls as the step shrinks, 121.3 at $\Delta t = 1$ then 96.0, 87.5
  and 83.7 at $0.1$, $0.05$ and $0.025$; mean final size goes 803.3, 683.5, 683.0,
  640.8. Freezing a step overstates infectiousness (recoveries late in a step
  still count for every contact in it) and delays transmission (new infections
  wait for the commit). At these settings the first wins, so the coarse step shows
  a net bias, not either effect alone.
- $\Delta t$ is both: at every finite value it defines frozen-step semantics, a
  different process, and shrinking it is how you approach the process intended.
  That $\Delta t = 1$ lands at 803.3, near the ODE's 800.2, is a coincidence of two
  unrelated errors.
- Every pair of ranges overlaps: 606 to 766 at $\Delta t = 0.1$ against 717 to 849
  at $\Delta t = 1$, so a single seed at each could have shown the effect
  backwards. The paired contrast is 119.8 with standard error 38.2, about three
  standard errors; the independent-sample 33.9 would be wrong here because the
  design is paired. Pairing gives the *larger* error because the correlation is
  $-0.285$.
- Below $\Delta t = 0.1$ the gaps (0.5 and 42.2) are well inside the spreads (67.9,
  40.4, 95.5), and $0.025$ against $0.1$ gives $-42.7$ with paired standard error
  49.9. Six seeds fail to detect a difference, which is not evidence of
  convergence. An ABM result is reported with its timestep, and a timestep chosen
  for runtime is a modelling decision made for a computational reason.

### Part D — how much the neighbourhood matters

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-d1
introduction_seeds = 9000 .+ (1:200)

function final_size(seed; radius = 2, I0 = 1, Δt = 0.1, max_steps = 6000)
    model = initialize_model(seed; I0, radius, Δt)
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model)
        step!(model, 1)
    end
    infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model)
    error("epidemic still infectious after $max_steps steps; increase max_steps")
end

final_sizes = Dict(radius => [final_size(seed; radius) for seed in introduction_seeds]
                   for radius in (1, 2))

fizzled = Dict(radius => final_sizes[radius] .< 100 for radius in (1, 2))

fizzle_fraction = Dict(radius => mean(fizzled[radius]) for radius in (1, 2))
mass_action_prediction = γ / (β * c)

check("at radius 2 the fizzle fraction is near the mass-action 1/R₀",
      abs(fizzle_fraction[2] - mass_action_prediction) < 0.1)
check("at radius 1 it is nowhere near it",
      fizzle_fraction[1] - mass_action_prediction > 0.3)

(; mass_action_prediction,
   fizzle_radius_1 = fizzle_fraction[1],
   fizzle_radius_2 = fizzle_fraction[2])
```

A cutoff chosen by hand can manufacture the split it claims to find, so these
two cells check whether it sits in an empty range or cuts through data.

```{julia}

    fizzle_fraction = round(mean(final_sizes[radius] .< cutoff); digits = 3))

```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-d4
gap_between_modes = [(; radius,
    largest_fizzle = maximum(final_sizes[radius][fizzled[radius]]; init = 0),
    smallest_takeoff = any(took_off[radius]) ?
        minimum(final_sizes[radius][took_off[radius]]) : nothing,
    in_the_middle = count(100 .<= final_sizes[radius] .<= 400),
    nearest_to_overall_mean =
        final_sizes[radius][argmin(abs.(final_sizes[radius] .- mean(final_sizes[radius])))],
    largest_outcome = maximum(final_sizes[radius]))
    for radius in (1, 2)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-introductions
#| fig-cap: "Final epidemic size across 200 introductions of a single infectious person, at contact radius 1 and radius 2. At radius 1 the outcomes form a single continuous spread of small outbreaks, none of them reaching a fifth of the population. At radius 2 they fall into two separated groups, and just under half of the runs land in the large one."

for (j, radius) in enumerate((1, 2))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; xlabel = "final number recovered", ylabel = "runs",
              title = "contact radius $radius")

fig
```

The same experiment with ten initial cases, at both radii, answers the third
question by measurement.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-d5
ten_case_seeds = 9500 .+ (1:50)

function ten_case_size(seed; radius, max_steps = 6000)
    model = initialize_model(seed; I0 = 10, radius = radius)
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model)
        step!(model, 1)
    end
    infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model)
    error("epidemic still infectious after $max_steps steps")
end

ten_case_sizes = Dict(radius => [ten_case_size(s; radius = radius)
                                 for s in ten_case_seeds]
                      for radius in (1, 2))

ten_case_summary = [(; radius,
    below_100 = mean(ten_case_sizes[radius] .< 100),
    smallest = minimum(ten_case_sizes[radius]),
    largest = maximum(ten_case_sizes[radius]),
    mean_size = round(mean(ten_case_sizes[radius]); digits = 1))
    for radius in (1, 2)]
```

#### D1. Interpret

- Only the neighbourhood changed: eight people at radius 1, twenty-four at
  radius 2. At radius 2, 55.5% of 200 single introductions finish below 100
  infections against the branching-process $1/R_0 = 0.5$, about one and a half
  standard errors apart, and the cutoff sits in an empty stretch between two
  groups. At radius 1, 96% finish below it, and that number describes the cutoff
  rather than establishment.
- $\beta c/\gamma = 2$ is the *mass-action* reproduction number. On a grid,
  repeated contacts land on the same few people, neighbours share neighbours, and
  an infective is soon ringed by the recovered. With twenty-four neighbours those
  corrections are small; with eight, most introductions stay a small cluster and
  the largest of the 200 reaches 168. The same three rates give different
  reproduction numbers on different contact structures.
- At radius 2, `mean_if_it_takes_off` is 634.0 and `mean_over_all_runs` 285.0.
  The outcomes split into 111 runs at or below 76 and 79 above 400, with 10 in
  between, and `gap_between_modes` places the empty stretch between 76 and 166.
  The overall mean lands in the sparse middle and describes neither group; the
  conditional mean and the fizzle fraction describe the two things that happen.
- At radius 1 the fizzle fraction moves from 0.66 at a cutoff of 20 to 0.96 at
  100, and the largest "fizzle" (93) sits next to the smallest "takeoff" (100):
  the cutoff cuts through data. Eight runs do exceed it, at 100 to 168, but the
  outcomes run continuously with no separation, so there is no evidence of an
  established-epidemic mode. Two hundred runs cannot exclude a rare one. At
  radius 2 cutoffs from 20 to 200 all give 0.520 to 0.560.
- From ten cases, 2% of runs finish below 100 at radius 2 against 55.5% from one,
  and 32% at radius 1 against 96%. Independent chains would predict
  $0.555^{10}$, under half a per cent, and $0.96^{10} \approx 0.67$; the chains
  share one grid and compete for susceptibles, and the cutoff applies to the
  total, which at radius 1 averages 158 (29 to 319), consistent with several
  clusters adding up.
- Ten starting cases conceal the single-introduction question, which is why
  Parts A to C showed none of it. Whether an introduction goes anywhere is decided
  while the counts are in single figures.
- *Stochastic* models earn their cost when counts are small and a probability is
  the answer wanted; the jump-process session already estimates extinction
  without representing anybody individually. *Agent-based and spatial* models
  earn their additional cost when contact structure changes those probabilities
  materially, and here the same $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ move the fraction below
  the cutoff from 0.555 to 0.96.
